newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/mark starts firm in Europe after Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark starts firm in Europe after Greenspan.

text.p: The dollar made a firm start against the mark in Europe, buoyed from its overnight gains on the back of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's comments that, for now, U.S. growth seems to be slowing.
The dollar climbed to 1.8245 marks in New York trade, its highest level since August 1991, as U.S. stocks and bonds soared amid the prospect of steady U.S. interest rates in the foreseeable future.
The dollar calmed down in Asian trade but was climbing back above 1.82 marks in early European dealings.

Analysts said Greenspan's testimony also indicated the Federal Reserve's satisfaction with the dollar's strength. The strong dollar was helping curb inflation, and high dollar demand meant the current account gap was not a problem, said Greenspan.
As well as the Greenspan factor, dollar/mark continued to find support from the general mark weakness and the ongoing uncertainty over European monetary union.

"With structural problems remaining untackled in Europe, the higher dollar will find few opponents on this side of the Atlantic," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.

"Greenspan has painted a very nice picture of the U.S. economy which is very bullish for U.S. asset markets," said Jesper Dannesboe, treasury economist at ABN-Amro in London. "The strong growth and low inflation scenario is also quite bullish for the dollar."

Greenspan, in his semiannual Humphrey-Hawkins report to Congress, said the current stance of monetary policy may have to be changed at some point but, at the present, demand growth appeared to have moderated.
His remarks saw the Dow close up 155 points and U.S. T-bond yields shrink to a near eight-month low of 6.44 percent.
Concern about a broad-based EMU and the ongoing perception of a soft euro continued to weigh on the mark, which posted new lows against non-EMU currencies.

Sterling/mark touched its highest level since September 1989, mark/Swiss franc held just above Tuesday's 10-month low and the mark slumped to its lowest levels against the Swedish crown since October 1992. Mark/yen slumped to a fresh 23-month low.
The mark showed some stability on its EMU crosses. Though weak, it was holding steady in morning Europe against the French franc, the lira and the peseta.

The recent break above 1.82 marks has re-ignited some concern of central bank intervention to cap the dollar, but this is less of a prospect now than a week ago when dollar/mark wrestled with the key 1.80 level.

"No doubt we will get the German authorities saying they are in contact with their G7 partners, but central banks are more astute and intervention now would be as effective as whistling against the wind," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest Markets in London.
By 0725 GMT, dollar/mark was trading at 1.8211/16 against 1.8168/78 late Tuesday in Europe.
Dollar/yen was firm but dealers said yen strength, especially against the mark, was keeping a lid on gains.
Agaisnt the yen, the dollar stood at 115.45/48 from 115.52/57 late Tuesday in Europe.
